item.title: An Unusual Conch | Nat Geo Photo of the Day
item.description:
An Unusual Conch

The arthritic spider conch (Harpago arthriticus) is native to the shallow waters in the Indian and western Pacific oceans. The image is part of Jim Wehtje's upcoming exhibit at the Bailey-Matthews National Shell Museum in Sanibel, Florida. Wehtje is primarily an x-ray photographer of plants and shells, but this project gave him room to expand. "I thought my life would be making only x-ray images, but I dusted off the camera and found surface and color again," he told National Geographic.

Jim Wehtje
item.author: Jim Wehtje

item.title: On the Court | Nat Geo Photo of the Day
item.description:
On the Court

Members of Jeddah United, the first Saudi sports league to include athletes of both genders, practice basketball. The company was founded in 2003 by Lina Khaled Almaeena and is training academy and sports league for both basketball and soccer. Photographer Lynsey Addario has spent more than a decade documenting the life of women in Saudi Arabia. “I want people to learn—to have a better sense of what Saudi women’s lives are,” she told National Geographic in 2016. “I hope people walk away with a different perspective.”

Lynsey Addario, Nat Geo Image Collection
item.author: Lynsey Addario, Nat Geo Image Collection

item.title: Amidst the Glow | Nat Geo Photo of the Day
item.description:
Amidst the Glow

The northern lights shine behind an abandoned homestead near Crawford, Nebraska. The light display can sometimes be seen in the Nebraska Panhandle, but only during strong geomagnetic storms, which happen just a few times a year. Also known as aurora borealis, the northern lights result from the collision of the sun's ions with gas atoms in Earth's atmosphere, which then releases particles of light in different colors.

Erik Johnson
item.author: Erik Johnson

item.title: The Horseback Riders | Nat Geo Photo of the Day
item.description:
The Horseback Riders

Two horseback riders prepare for the "Just Jumpers Horse Show" at the Three County Fair in Northampton, Massachusetts. The event is the oldest continuously operating agricultural fair in the United States and sees thousands of attendees annually. The fair hosts several horse competitions, including the New England Morgan Horse Show, where visitors can watch everything from carriage driving to ranch work take place.

Nat Segebre
item.author: Nat Segebre

item.title: Hard at Work | Nat Geo Photo of the Day
item.description:
Hard at Work

Builders work on construction of the South-North Water Transfer Project in the Shandong Province in China. Launched in 2002 with completion expected in 2050, the project's goal is to move trillions of gallons of water each year from the Yangtze River Basin in the south to the Yellow River Basin in the north. The relocation of the water is expected to help with both agricultural growth and domestic water supply in the dry northern region of the country—parts of which are also densely populated.

Michael S. Yamashita, Nat Geo Image Collection
item.author: Michael S. Yamashita, Nat Geo Image Collection

item.title: In the Tropics | Nat Geo Photo of the Day
item.description:
In the Tropics

A scarlet macaw (Ara macao) hangs from a tree in Tikal National Park, Guatemala. The bird is native to subtropical rainforests across Central and South America and is classified as endangered due to various threats, including the illegal wildlife trade. While the average lifespan of a scarlet macaw in the wild is between 40 and 50 years, they can live up to 75 years in captivity. In 2014, National Geographic reported on the relocation efforts of Mexican scarlet macaws in order to save them from poachers.

Wesley Colvin
item.author: Wesley Colvin

item.title: Snacks Galore | Nat Geo Photo of the Day
item.description:
Snacks Galore

Rows of colorful snacks and dried foods fill the shelves of an Aji Ichiban store in Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon, Hong Kong. Francesca Forquet snapped this photo in December 2012, as she became acquainted with the city—"its density, its complexity, and the constant feeling of not knowing what I would find around the next corner," she tells National Geographic. At the time, the local snack chain had over a hundred locations. The loss of tourist traffic during the pandemic led to the closure of all Aji Ichiban locations in the city 10 years later.

Francesca Forquet
item.author: Francesca Forquet

item.title: One With the Earth | Nat Geo Photo of the Day
item.description:
One With the Earth

Iceland's grassy landscape envelops the Hofskirkja church in Fagurhólsmýri. The church was built in 1884 and is one of six constructed in this style, with the earthen enclosure naturally cooling the space in the summer and warming it in the winter. Photographer Flip Twogood has a fondness for Iceland's churches. "They all have such a unique aesthetic, and this one was incredible with the grass-covered roof and crosses in the ground," he tells National Geographic.

Flip Twogood
item.author: Flip Twogood

item.title: Ready for Take Off | Nat Geo Photo of the Day
item.description:
Ready for Take Off

Erislandy is a Cuban pigeon racer known throughout Old Havana for dyeing his birds like the one pictured here in fluorescent colors. The sport, known as colombofilia, has grown in popularity on the island. Photographer Carlos Jaramillo met Erislandy just after discovering he was not of Cuban heritage as he had always believed; his photo project, Picadero, not only documents pigeon racing in Cuba, but also his budding relationship with Erislandy in this time of reckoning with his cultural identity.

Carlos Jaramillo
item.author: Carlos Jaramillo

item.title: On the Surface | Nat Geo Photo of the Day
item.description:
On the Surface

Trapped air bubbles form on the surface of still water in a small moorland in the Sachsenwald Forest near Hamburg, Germany. Jan Erik Waider's image shows the natural patterns of green and yellow, as well as varying textures, created by the algae and aquatic plants sitting just beneath the translucent bubbles. These patterns are shaped by growth, decay, and changing conditions in the water.

Jan Erik Waider
item.author: Jan Erik Waider
